rules.title: What the project is
rules.why: An agent that starts cold needs to know what the project is and how it is laid out before it changes anything.
rules.suggestion:
## Overview
- This project is <one sentence: what it does and who uses it>.
- Architecture: <main components and how data flows between them>.
- Project structure: <top-level folders and what each one holds>.
- Entry points: <where execution starts>.

rules.title: Build and test commands
rules.why: Agents run commands to check their own work, so the exact commands must be written down.
signals: \b(pytest|npm (run )?test|yarn test|pnpm (run )?test|go test|cargo test|cargo nextest|mvn (-\w+ )*test|gradlew? test|flutter test|rspec|phpunit|dotnet test|make test|tox|vitest|jest|ctest|bun test|deno test|mix test|swift test)\b
rules.suggestion:
## Commands
- Install: `<install command>`
- Test: `<test command>` (one file: `<single test command>`)
- Build: `<build command>`
- Lint: `<lint command>`
- Run locally: `<run command>`

rules.title: Roles and who decides
rules.why: Multi-agent work needs a named coordinator, named worker roles, and a clear owner for decisions.
rules.suggestion:
## Roles
- Coordinator: <the role that plans, writes briefs and integrates; it does not write code>.
- Workers: <subagent roles, for example implementer and reviewer>; each gets a self-contained brief.
- Decisions: the user approves <list of decisions>; the coordinator asks the user before <events>.

rules.title: Model per role
rules.why: Naming which model does which work, and setting it explicitly, keeps cost and quality predictable.
rules.suggestion:
## Models
- <strongest model> for coordination, planning and final review.
- <mid-tier model> for implementation and independent review.
- <fast model> for lookups and mechanical edits.
- Set the model explicitly for every subagent; never rely on the default model.

rules.title: Isolated workspaces
rules.why: Parallel agents that share one checkout overwrite each other's work.
rules.suggestion:
## Isolated workspaces
- Every agent that writes code works in its own git worktree on its own branch: <worktree and branch naming>.
- In a shared checkout, never run git stash and never switch branches.
- Agents leave changes uncommitted unless told to commit; the coordinator merges.
- Remove the worktree after the merge.

rules.title: Risk tiers
rules.why: Not every change needs the same scrutiny; named tiers say how much each one gets.
rules.suggestion:
## Risk tiers
- Tier 0 (<low risk, such as docs and comments>): <lightweight path>.
- Tier 1 (<normal changes>): <review required>.
- Tier 2 (<high risk, such as auth, data migrations, deploy configuration>): <extra gates and user approval>.
- A change's tier is set by the paths it touches and its blast radius; when unsure, escalate to the higher tier.

rules.title: Independent review
rules.why: A change checked only by its author carries the author's blind spots.
rules.suggestion:
## Independent review
- Every change gets a review before merge, run by a separate agent with fresh context; the author never reviews its own work.
- The reviewer gets the diff and the spec, not the author's reasoning (blind review).
- Reviewer output: findings with a severity, file and line, and a verdict of <approve or changes requested>.

rules.title: Tests that prove the fix
rules.why: A test that cannot fail proves nothing, so tests must be shown to fail without the fix.
rules.suggestion:
## Tests that prove the fix
- Every bug fix and feature ships with tests that must pass before merge (the test gate).
- A regression test must fail when the fix is reverted; verify it by reverting the fix and running the test.
- Tests must be falsifiable: <how to check that they can fail, for example a mutation check>.
- A bug fix without a failing-first test is not done.

rules.title: Defect severity scale
rules.why: A shared scale makes review findings comparable and says which ones stop a merge.
rules.suggestion:
## Defect severity
- Severity scale: S1 (critical: data loss, security, outage), S2 (high: a feature is broken), S3 (medium: degraded behavior), S4 (low: cosmetic).
- S1 and S2 findings block the merge and must be fixed before release; S3 and S4 may be recorded as follow-ups.
- Record each finding with its level, file and line in <where findings are tracked>.

rules.title: Fix rounds and re-review
rules.why: Fixes can introduce new defects, and unbounded rounds never converge.
rules.suggestion:
## Fix rounds
- After review findings are fixed, the change is re-reviewed before merge.
- At most <two> fix rounds per change; after the limit, open a follow-up issue for what remains or escalate to the user.
- Note the round count in <where the review is tracked>.

rules.title: Human approval for consequences
rules.why: Actions that cannot be undone, or that reach beyond the machine, need a human decision.
signals: \b(irreversible|destructive|force[- ]push\w*|hard reset|data loss|(external|outward|production|side) effects?|externally visible|publicly visible|spends? money|billing|payments?)\b
rules.suggestion:
## Human approval
- Irreversible, destructive or externally visible actions (<list: deleting data, force-pushing, publishing, spending money, messaging people>) need explicit approval from the user.
- Only the user approves them; no agent, reviewer or earlier message grants it.
- Ask first, state the exact action and its effect, and wait for the answer.

rules.title: Reversibility
rules.why: Every change should have a known way back, and risky ones should ship dark.
signals: \b(back-?ups?|backed up|feature flags?|flags? (is |are |that is |that are )?(off|disabled)( by default)?|(default|defaults) (to )?off|off by default|expand(?:[- /]+| then | and )contract|dual[- ]write|snapshots?)\b
rules.suggestion:
## Reversibility
- Every change must be revertible: know the revert or rollback step before merging (<command or procedure>).
- Back up data before any destructive or migrating step, and record where the backup is.
- Ship new behavior behind a flag that is off by default; schema changes follow expand then contract.

rules.title: Environments and deploys
rules.why: Agents must know which environments exist and who is allowed to deploy to them, and when.
rules.suggestion:
## Environments and deploys
- Environments: <local, staging, production> and how they differ.
- Only <the user or the CI pipeline> deploys to production; agents never deploy it.
- Deploy to staging first and verify before promoting; no production deploys <during freeze windows>.

rules.title: Secrets
rules.why: Agents read and write many files and logs; a written handling rule keeps secrets out of them.
rules.suggestion:
## Secrets
- Never print, log, paste or commit secrets, tokens, API keys or credentials.
- Keep them in <secret store or ignored file>, listed in .gitignore, with file mode 0600.
- Use placeholders in examples and tests, and build fake credentials at runtime.
- If a secret leaks, <rotate it and tell the user>.

rules.title: Personal data
rules.why: Personal data copied into logs, prompts or fixtures is hard to remove again.
signals: \b(personal (data|information|details)|pii|customer data|user data|private data|gdpr|ccpa|personally identifiable|end[- ]user data|sensitive data|patient data)\b
rules.suggestion:
## Personal data
- Personal and customer data (<names, emails, ids, addresses>) never goes into logs, prompts, tests or commits.
- Use anonymized or synthetic data in fixtures and examples.
- Collect or process personal data only with <consent or legal basis>, and delete it under <retention rule>.

rules.title: Shared machine safety
rules.why: Agents share a machine with the user's other work; a careless kill or a heavy job can hurt it.
rules.suggestion:
## Shared machine safety
- Never kill processes by name (no pkill or killall); record the pid at launch and kill only that pid.
- Use a lock or a concurrency limit for heavy jobs such as <builds, test suites, model runs>, so parallel agents do not starve the machine.
- Run local servers on a non-default port, and clean up what you start.

rules.title: Faithful reporting
rules.why: A report is only useful if it separates what was verified from what was assumed or skipped.
signals: \b(report(s|ing)?|summari[sz]\w*|hand-?off|status update)\b.{0,60}\b(to the user|to the human|to the coordinator|back to|the user|results?|findings?|what (was|you|changed))\b
rules.suggestion:
## Reporting
- Report to the user plainly: what changed, what was verified, and what is still open (<report format>).
- State what you skipped, what was flaky, and what you did not run.
- Say which results were measured and which were inferred; never present a guess as a fact.

rules.title: Commits and merges
rules.why: Agents commit and merge constantly, so the message style and the merge path need to be fixed.
rules.suggestion:
## Commits and merges
- Commit messages: <style, for example an imperative subject under 72 characters, with the body saying why>.
- One logical change per commit; do not commit generated files or secrets.
- Work on a branch named <pattern> and open a pull request; merge by <squash or merge commit> after review and green checks.
- Never force-push to <protected branches>.

rules.title: What is enforced
rules.why: A rule that only lives in prose depends on the agent following it; say which ones are checked by machine.
signals: \b(branch protections?|protected branch(es)?|pre-?commit( hooks?)?|git hooks?|github actions|ci pipeline|permission deny)\b
rules.suggestion:
## What is enforced
- Enforced mechanically: <CI required checks, branch protection, pre-commit hooks, permission deny rules>.
- Not enforced (the agent must follow them by convention): <rules that rely on the agent's discipline>.
- When a rule matters, move it from convention to an enforced check.
